children: By Collin Eaton and Benoît Morenne
ExxonMobil is close to signing a preliminary deal to explore investments in several Venezuelan oil fields, negotiating a potential return to the country nearly two decades after its exit.

Exxon could sign a memorandum of understanding with state-run Petróleos de Venezuela as soon as this month to explore a deal to invest in a number of developed and undeveloped fields, according to people familiar with the matter. The deal talks could still fall apart or extend beyond September, the people said.

The deal could encompass fields that collectively have 50 billion barrels of oil buried underground, one of the people said. Venezuela says it has around 300 billion barrels of oil reserves, which would make its reserves the largest in the world.

The U.S. oil giant has sent teams to Caracas this year to negotiate a possible deal following President Trump's push for American oil producers to revitalize the Latin American country's rundown oil sector. The company has inched closer to a deal with Venezuelan officials over time and was expected to continue those talks at the G-20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston this week, one of the other people said.

Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others have tried to recenter the global energy industry in the Western Hemisphere, prodding companies to pour $100 billion in Venezuela to bolster its depressed crude production and ship the oil to U.S. refineries.

Exxon's chief rival, Chevron, earlier this month inked a deal to invest $7 billion in Venezuela over five years through its joint ventures there, aiming to double its output to 600,000 barrels a day. On Wednesday, billionaire oil baron Harold Hamm signed a preliminary deal to explore an undeveloped oil field in the state of Anzoátegui.

Several large oil-and-gas companies have hesitated to commit capital to Venezuela, wary of financial and legal problems that could arise in making yearslong investments in a country with a track record of nationalizing private companies' assets. Exxon and ConocoPhillips, the third-largest U.S. oil company, are both still seeking restitution for billions of dollars in losses following Hugo Chávez's move in 2007 to nationalize their assets.

During a televised White House meeting with Trump in January, Exxon CEO Darren Woods and others expressed caution. At the time, Woods said Venezuela appeared to be "uninvestable" without significant changes to the country's commercial frameworks, legal system and hydrocarbon laws.

Venezuela has since overhauled oil-related regulations, including allowing for lower tax rates on oil production. In a press release Wednesday, Continental cited the country's recent changes to regulatory and legal framework as one of the reasons it was able to move forward with a deal.
